implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Specify needs
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This phase is triggered when a need for new statistics is identified, perhaps resulting from user feedback, or a review is undertaken. It includes all activities associated with engaging stakeholders to identify their detailed statistical needs (current or future), proposing high level solution options and preparing a business case, which may weigh the benefits of addressing these needs against expected costs, risks and other requirements, considering the public good arising from meeting those needs and the implications for respondents, users and other stakeholders. The Specify Needs phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 7), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This phase is triggered when a need for new statistics is identified, perhaps resulting from user feedback, or a review is undertaken. It includes all activities associated with engaging stakeholders to identify their detailed statistical needs (current or future), proposing high level solution options, and preparing a business case. In the modernized statistical environment, these activities are increasingly supported by automated and AI-powered processes—ranging from the synthesis and structuring of stakeholder inputs, through the analysis of options, to the automated drafting of business case materials. Routine and repetitive aspects of needs identification, consultation, and documentation are minimized for manual intervention, enabling staff to focus on higher-value tasks: interpreting context, establishing priorities, and making strategic decisions that cannot be automated. The phase thus leverages end-to-end process automation and AI wherever possible, supporting greater efficiency, responsiveness, and quality at the earliest stage of the statistical business process. The Specify Needs phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 7), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' participates in 'the analysis of statistical program data,' 'suggests possible feedback on collection... and assists in the development of recommendations for improvements to survey methods and activities.' As needs investigation becomes automated, this role adapts from manual environmental scanning to 'assessing the validity of collected and processed data,' now largely in partnership with AI and automated feedback synthesis. Their responsibilities for analyzing feedback, preparing recommendations, and interpreting user needs are now less about manual collation and more about oversight, validation, and nuanced contextualization of AI findings. Their knowledge of data flows and evaluation techniques will be directed toward managing and supervising AI-driven inputs and focusing effort on the highest value-add problems.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Identify needs
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process includes the initial investigation and identification of what statistics are needed and what is needed of the statistics. It may be triggered by a new information request from users, an environmental change such as a reduced budget, a periodic review, or respondent feedback. Action plans from evaluations of previous iterations of the production cycle (including from respondent feedback) or from other programmes might provide an input to this sub-process. It also includes consideration of practice amongst other (national and international) statistical organisations producing similar data and the methods used by those organisations.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process includes the initial investigation and identification of what statistics are needed and what is needed of the statistics. In the modern process, AI and automated tools are used to continuously scan for new information requests from users, detect relevant environmental changes, and aggregate respondent feedback and evaluation action plans. These technologies also benchmark needs by automatically referencing practices among other (national and international) statistical organizations. Automation supports the collation, analysis, and structuring of these triggers for new or changed statistics, while staff focus their expertise on interpreting context, confirming significance, and ensuring response to complex or emergent requirements.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' participates in 'the analysis of statistical program data,' 'suggests possible feedback on collection... and assists in the development of recommendations for improvements to survey methods and activities.' As needs investigation becomes automated, this role adapts from manual environmental scanning to 'assessing the validity of collected and processed data,' now largely in partnership with AI and automated feedback synthesis.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Consult and confirm needs
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process focuses on consulting with the internal and external stakeholders and confirming in detail the needs for the statistics. A good understanding of user needs is required so that the statistical organisation knows not only what it is expected to deliver, but also when, how, and perhaps most importantly, why. For the second and subsequent iterations of this sub-process, the main focus will be on determining whether previously identified needs have changed. This detailed understanding of user needs is the critical part of this sub-process.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process focuses on consulting with internal and external stakeholders and confirming in detail the needs for the statistics. Automated and AI-supported systems are now used to organize and analyze input from stakeholders, including feedback, evolving requirements, and historical engagement. These tools facilitate discovery of patterns and highlight changes in user needs over time. Statistical staff engage directly where nuanced negotiation, detailed interpretation, or complex prioritization is required, ensuring that automated summaries and analytics are supplemented by expert, context-aware judgment. This detailed understanding of user needs and the efficient, technology-enabled consultation process are both critical to this sub-process.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' 'provides data and assistance to users, within and outside Statistics Canada.' In the context of automated feedback organization, this becomes a quality and prioritization oversight role for stakeholder requirements, rather than a manual aggregator. The work-description's emphasis on 'liaising with subject matter specialists and users to develop and translate requirements' aligns with consulting and confirming needs with AI assistance.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Establish output objectives
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process identifies the statistical output objectives that are required to meet the user needs confirmed in sub-process 1.2 (Consult and confirm needs). It includes agreeing the suitability of the proposed outputs and their quality measures with users. Legal or normative frameworks (e.g. relating to confidentiality, methodologies), and available resources are important to consider when establishing output objectives.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process identifies the statistical output objectives that are required to meet the user needs confirmed in sub-process 1.2 (Consult and confirm needs). AI and automated tools aggregate and analyze confirmed user requirements, historical deliverables, legal/normative frameworks, and available resource constraints to generate draft output objectives and candidate quality measures. Staff provide oversight by aligning these drafts with strategic intent, adjudicating complex trade-offs, and ensuring compliance with legal and methodological expectations. This shift supports more efficient, responsive, and high-quality output objective-setting by leveraging technology for foundational work and human expertise for final judgment and alignment.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' role of providing 'analysis of data and suggests possible feedback on collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures, and assists in the development of recommendations' is directly relevant. Their focus shifts to confirming appropriateness of AI-proposed output objectives, ensuring compliance with standards and legal requirements.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Identify concepts
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process clarifies the required concepts to be measured from the point of view of the users. At this stage, the concepts identified might not align with existing statistical standards. This alignment, and the choice or definition of the statistical and other concepts and variables to be used, takes place in sub-process 2.2 (Design variables).
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process clarifies the required concepts to be measured from the point of view of the users. Automated and AI-assisted tools are leveraged to synthesize user requirements, prior documentation, and relevant internal/external sources, providing preliminary suggestions and structured options for possible concepts. The role of the subject matter sponsor is central—this person or group is solely accountable for the final specification and formal certification of the required concepts prior to downstream design or standard alignment. This approach minimizes manual tasks, maintains clear accountability, and increases speed and efficiency in the establishment of robust conceptual frameworks.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The update highlights two changes: (1) AI/automation supports 'synthesize user requirements, prior documentation, and relevant internal/external sources,' and (2) the 'subject matter sponsor is solely accountable' for final specification and certification. The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' must now validate AI-suggested concepts and is accountable for final specification, as the work-description specifies knowledge of 'statistical or economic theory and principles... and methods and techniques of data gathering, statistical estimation...' and liaising to 'develop and translate subject-matter requirements into specifications for system development.' Their responsibilities now heavily involve overseeing AI-supported proposals, certifying their validity, and documenting concept definition for downstream design.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Check data availability and suitability
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process checks whether current sources of data could meet user requirements and the conditions under which they would be available, including any restrictions on their use. An assessment of possible alternatives would normally include research into potential administrative or other non-statistical sources of data (e.g. privately-held data or “Big Data”), to: Determine whether they would be suitable for use for statistical purposes (e.g. the extent to which administrative concepts match data requirements, and whether the timeliness and quality of the data, security, and continuity of data supply are suitable); Assess the division of responsibilities between data suppliers and the statistical organisation; Check necessary ICT resources (e.g. data storage, technology required to handle incoming data and data processing) as well as any provision agreements with data suppliers (which could be legal or other agreements such as memoranda of understanding) for accessing and sharing the data (e.g. formats, delivery, accompanying metadata and quality check). When existing sources have been assessed, a strategy for filling any remaining gaps in the data requirement is prepared. This may include identifying possible partnerships with data holders or conducting a new survey to collect data if necessary. This sub-process also includes a more general assessment of the legal framework in which data would be collected and used, and may therefore identify proposals for changes to existing legislation or the introduction of a new legal framework.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process systematically checks whether current sources of data could meet user requirements and the conditions under which they would be available, including any restrictions on their use. Existing data holdings must be exhaustively investigated and prioritized first, followed by a search for relevant administrative and alternative data sources; the option to conduct new surveys is only considered if these avenues prove insufficient to meet data needs. The subject matter sponsor holds sole accountability for certifying that all relevant avenues for data have been thoroughly explored and that the suitability, timeliness, and quality of any proposed source have been rigorously assessed. To expedite and strengthen the acquisition of administrative and alternative data, a center of expertise works collaboratively with subject matter specialists to support negotiations, acquisition logistics, and the establishment of legal or operational agreements where needed. When multiple avenues have been assessed and documented, a strategy for filling any remaining gaps is prepared. This sub-process also encompasses the assessment and possible updates to the legal framework for data collection, ensuring fit-for-purpose, respondent-efficient, and timely data acquisition and usage.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: With the update, the process must now 'formalize a strict hierarchy of data sourcing—first considering existing data holdings, then administrative and alternative data, and only lastly, new survey data collection.' Further, the 'subject matter sponsor holds sole accountability,' and a 'center of expertise works collaboratively.' The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' is deeply implicated, as their work-description emphasizes assessing the 'validity of collected and processed data,' and 'analyzes current collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods and procedures to ascertain their relevancy and to propose changes or alternative systems.' They must now systematically evaluate automated outputs about available data sources, certify the thoroughness and suitability, and partner with the designated data acquisition teams.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Prepare and submit business case
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process documents the findings of the other sub-processes in this phase, in the form of a business case to get approval to implement the new or modified statistical business process. Such a business case would need to conform to the requirements of the approval body, but would typically include elements such as: A description of the “As-Is” business process (if it already exists), with information on how the current statistics are produced, highlighting any inefficiencies and issues to be addressed; The proposed “To-Be” solution, detailing how the statistical business process will be developed to produce the new or revised statistics; An assessment of costs and benefits against objectives and any external constraints. The business case describes options and makes recommendations. It may include the benefits, costs, deliverables, time frame, budget, required technical and human resources, risk assessment and impact on stakeholders for each option. After the business case is prepared, it is submitted for approval to move to the next phase of the business process. At this sub-process, a “go”/“no go” decision is made. Typically, the business case is reviewed and formally approved or disapproved by the appropriate sponsors and governance committees.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process documents the findings of the other sub-processes in this phase in the form of a business case to get approval to implement a new or modified statistical business process. In the contemporary process, automated and AI-driven systems are used to collate, analyze, and generate initial drafts for all key business case sections—including the description of the 'As-Is' process, the proposed 'To-Be' solution, and the relevant assessments of cost, benefit, risks, deliverables, and impact. Staff and sponsors then review, contextualize, and refine these drafts, ensuring proper alignment with strategic objectives and organizational needs before final submission. The business case is reviewed and approved by the relevant body, with human expertise providing the final evaluation and decision. By leveraging automation, the preparation of business cases gains efficiency and speed, allowing human effort to be concentrated on strategic oversight and quality assurance.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' is implicated as their role includes 'providing data and assistance to users... participates in the analysis of data... and assists in the development of recommendations for improvements to survey methods and activities.' As AI/automation assembles business case materials, their expertise enables strategic review—ensuring all options, risks, and contextual implications are properly articulated and substantiated.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Design
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This phase describes the development and design activities, and any associated practical research work needed to define the statistical outputs, variables, methodologies, collection instruments and operational processes, with due regard to other requirements such as security. It includes all the design elements needed to define or refine the statistical products or services identified in the business case. This phase specifies all relevant metadata, in accordance with the standards and corporate policies, ready for use later in the business process, as well as quality assurance procedures. For statistical outputs produced on a regular basis, this phase usually occurs for the first iteration and whenever improvement actions are identified in the Evaluate phase of a previous iteration. Design activities make substantial use of international and national standards in order to reduce the length and cost of the design process, and enhance interoperability, comparability, etc. Organisations may reuse or adapt design elements from existing processes and consider geospatial aspects of data in the design to enhance the usability and value of the statistical information. Additionally, outputs of design processes may form the basis for future standards at the organisational, national or international levels. The Design phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 8), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative. Some approaches used to develop tools and systems involve iteration between sub-processes in the Design and Build phases.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This phase describes the development and design activities, and any associated practical research work needed to define the statistical outputs, variables, methodologies, collection instruments, and operational processes—with a strong emphasis on automation, AI-powered tools, and digital interoperability. Automated and AI-driven processes play a central role in drafting specifications, aligning with corporate and international standards, generating and enriching metadata, simulating system interactions, and iterating design improvements. All statistical products and their supporting metadata are produced in standardized, richly described, and machine-actionable forms, ensuring they are interoperable and reusable across downstream tools, APIs, and organizational systems. Staff are freed from repetitive and routine design work and instead focus on innovation, calibration, and optimizing for evolving user and stakeholder requirements. Design activities thus promote efficiency, quality, and discoverability, embedding best practices for automation, standardization, and open data access. The Design phase is broken down into six sub-processes (Figure 8), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, can occur in parallel, and may be iterative. Iteration between Design and Build phases is supported through automated versioning and process enhancements.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' is implicated through 'analysis of data and assistance in the preparation of analytical material,' and 'suggests possible feedback on collection, processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods.' With digital-first and standardization the norm, they focus on the review, strategic selection, and adaptation of standards-embedded designs and automated metadata outputs—for both methodological integrity and fit-for-purpose analytical use.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Design processing and analysis
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process designs the statistical methodology to be applied during the Process and Analyse phases. This can include, among others, specification of routines and rules for coding, editing and imputation, which may vary based on the means of data collection and source of data. This subprocess also includes design of specifications for data integration from multiple data sources, validation of data and estimation. Statistical disclosure control methods are also designed here if they are specific to this business process.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process designs the statistical methodology to be applied during the Process and Analyse phases, with a core emphasis on standards-based automation, AI enablement, and digital interoperability. Specifications for routines and rules covering coding, editing, imputation, validation, and data integration/estimation are required to be implemented, where practical, using automated frameworks and AI/ML-driven tools—leveraging SDMX models, .STAT processing, and corporate-standard solutions (e.g., Aria/Colectica). Human analysts and methodologists are focused on reviewing and updating analytic methods for non-standard or novel use-cases, with all standardizable and repeatable components digital, automated, and reproducible by default. Statistical disclosure control and quality assurance methods designed here also leverage automation and AI for rapid, secure, and scalable deployment. All methodologies are documented to be compatible with downstream digital workflows and to support auditing, versioning, and continuous improvement.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' is also implicated for a similar reason: they have 'knowledge of methods and techniques of data gathering, statistical estimation and economic modeling,' and 'evaluate and propose changes to processing, editing, compilation and presentation methods.' Their responsibilities expand into the oversight of AI-implemented methodologies, reviewing digital pipelines for theoretical rigor and ensuring all analysis routines are standards-compliant by design.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Analyse
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: In this phase, statistical outputs are produced and examined in detail. It includes preparing statistical content (including commentary, technical notes, etc.), and ensuring outputs are “fit for purpose” prior to dissemination to users. This phase also includes the sub-processes and activities that enable statistical analysts to understand the data and the statistics produced. The outputs of this phase could also be used as an input to other sub-processes (e.g. analysis of new sources as input to the Design phase). For statistical outputs produced regularly, this phase occurs in every iteration. The Analyse phase and sub-processes are generic for all statistical outputs, regardless of how the data were sourced. The Analyse phase is broken down into five sub-processes (Figure 12), which are presented sequentially, from left to right, but can also occur in parallel, and can be iterative.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: In this phase, statistical outputs are produced and examined in detail using automated, AI-powered, and modular analytical pipelines. All workflows—from draft output and commentary preparation to validation and finalization—leverage digital automation and AI/ML-driven solutions, producing real-time, reproducible, and version-controlled results. Automated generation of daily write-ups, dashboards, and other standardized products is the norm, with human analysts focused on interpretation, contextualization, and providing tailored, nuanced analysis for users. Intelligent, real-time validation and anomaly detection are embedded throughout. The phase is fully iterative and feedback-driven, supporting rapid, responsive, and continuous analytic enhancement. The Analyse phase and its sub-processes are applicable to all outputs regardless of data source, and support the seamless transition to dissemination.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: GSBPM updates require 'automated, AI-powered, and modular analytical pipelines' for output creation and validation, with human analysts focusing on contextualization, interpretation, and communicating nuanced findings. The 'Economist/Sociologist 2', whose work includes 'participates in the analysis of statistical program data,' 'assists in the preparation of analytical material,' and 'identifies statistical trends and developments,' will increasingly oversee, review, and contextualize AI-generated analyses rather than perform manual computation. They will focus on providing advanced subject-matter interpretation, tailoring output explanations for users, and innovating in analytic commentary.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Prepare draft outputs
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process is where the data from sub-processes 5.7 (Calculate aggregates) and 5.8 (Finalise data files) are transformed into statistical outputs, which could include indexes, seasonally adjusted statistics, mapped data, microdata, etc. The preparation of maps, GIS outputs and geo-statistical services can be included to maximise the value and capacity to analyse the statistical information. Methodological notes, to accompany the outputs and describe how they have been produced are also prepared in this sub-process taking as input the methodology designed in the Design phase. When new processing or analysis methods such as those based on machine learning or artificial intelligence are used, additional explanations might need to be prepared to communicate/explain the necessary information to the users.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process transforms processed and finalized data into statistical outputs using automated, AI-powered pipelines. Outputs—including indices, seasonally adjusted statistics, mapped data, geo-statistical services, write-ups, dashboards, and methodological documentation—are generated by default through LLM/AI-driven automation. Human analysts intervene to interpret, refine, or tailor outputs for specialized, complex, or critical communication needs. AI-generated methodological notes and narratives accompany all outputs, documenting analytic approaches and logic. This automation-first approach maximizes efficiency, consistency, and allows analysts to focus on providing added value and insight.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: The sub-process is now 'AI-powered pipelines. Outputs—including indices, seasonally adjusted statistics, mapped data, geo-statistical services, write-ups, dashboards, and methodological documentation—are generated by default through LLM/AI-driven automation.' The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' ('participates in the analysis... and assists in the preparation of analytical material') is required to review, interpret, and contextualize automated outputs, ensure user-centric narrative, and tailor communication to nuanced or complex user needs.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Validate outputs
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process is where statisticians validate the outputs produced, in accordance with a general quality framework and with expectations and also comparing with auxiliary information available (e.g. from previous cycles or from other sources). This sub-process may include activities involved with the gathering of intelligence, with the cumulative effect of building up a body of knowledge about a specific statistical domain, in order to check for errors and validate the data as objectively as possible. This knowledge is then applied to the current collection, in the current environment, to identify any divergence from expectations and to allow informed analyses. Validation activities can include: Comparing the statistics with previous cycles (if applicable); Checking that the associated metadata, paradata and quality indicators are present and in line with expectations; Checking geospatial consistency of the data; Confronting the statistics against other relevant data (both internal and external); Investigating inconsistencies in the statistics; Performing macro editing; Checking aggregates as a validation for a microdata set; Validating the statistics against expectations and domain intelligence.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process is where outputs are validated using automated, AI- and ML-powered, real-time digital workflows. Anomaly detection, benchmarking against historical data, metadata and paradata checks, macro editing, and internal/external confrontations are executed with machine-driven QA and pattern recognition. Complex, novel, or ambiguous findings are escalated to human statistics experts for review and contextual analysis, ensuring that outputs are validated rapidly, consistently, and with high assurance of quality.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: Validation moves to 'automated, AI- and ML-powered, real-time digital workflows,' escalating only complex or unusual findings to human experts. The 'Economist/Sociologist 2', responsible for 'identifying statistical trends and developments' and 'participates in the analysis of data and suggests possible feedback on... editing, compilation and presentation methods,' will now focus on adjudicating anomalies, reviewing validation logic, and embedding domain intelligence into AI-supported validation processes.

implicated phases and sub-processes.title: Interpret and explain outputs
implicated phases and sub-processes.original description: This sub-process is where outputs are interpreted in order to understand their meaning and to try to explain them. This can involve viewing the statistics from all perspectives using different tools and media, and carrying out various types of in-depth analysis to gain insight into the results and assess them against initial expectations, based also on an understanding of how those results were produced. Such analyses might include time series analysis and other econometric analyses, etc.
implicated phases and sub-processes.updated description: This sub-process interprets and explains outputs using LLM/AI-powered narrative generation, visualization, and automated analytics to provide first-draft explanations and insight. Statisticians and analysts review and refine these drafts, supplementing them with domain expertise, context, and additional analytics as needed to make results accessible and meaningful, especially for nuanced or high-impact topics.
implicated phases and sub-processes.justification: GSBPM: 'LLMs offer insights and suggest explanations for complex statistical results, aiding human experts in making data accessible to non-technical audiences. They also provide visualizations and narrative explanations...' The 'Economist/Sociologist 2' must now review, refine, and supplement AI-generated narratives and visualizations, ensuring nuanced, accurate, and contextually salient interpretation of statistical outputs for a range of users.
